cards.front: Maximum lignocaine dose: [___] mg/kg plain, 7 mg/kg with adrenaline.
cards.context:
Plain lignocaine: 3 mg/kg max. Adrenaline (1:200,000) lifts this to 7 mg/kg by causing local vasoconstriction that slows systemic absorption.

For a 70 kg adult: 210 mg plain, 490 mg with adrenaline. Useful conversion: 1% lignocaine = 10 mg/mL, so 21 mL plain or 49 mL with adrenaline.

cards.front: RSTI NAC thresholds: paracetamol >20 mg/L OR ALT >50 U/L. The [___] does NOT apply to RSTI.
cards.context: RSTI management differs from acute overdose — the nomogram doesn't apply. Instead, use screening labs and clinical criteria to guide NAC.

cards.front: HFNO delivers flow rates up to [___] L/min and generates 2-5 cmH2O of CPAP effect.
cards.context:
HFNO delivers gas at 20-60 L/min — matching or exceeding peak inspiratory flow rates so the patient breathes only the delivered gas mixture (no room air entrainment). FiO2 can be set anywhere from 21-100%.

The high flow also generates a small amount of CPAP (2-5 cmH2O), stents the upper airway open, washes out nasopharyngeal dead space, and improves comfort through humidification and warming.

cards.front: CPP = MAP − [___], target 60-70 mmHg in TBI.
cards.context:
CPP is the driving pressure for cerebral blood flow. Too low causes secondary brain injury from ischaemia; too high requires excessive vasopressor support which increases pulmonary complications.

Balance is key.

cards.front: Normal lactate is below 2.0 mmol/L. Elevated lactate suggests tissue [___].
cards.context: Lactate over 2 in sepsis (with vasopressor need) defines septic shock. But lactate can also rise in seizures, metformin use, liver failure, or thiamine deficiency — context matters.

cards.front: A delta ratio >2 indicates a concurrent [___] on top of HAGMA.
cards.context: Without delta-delta, you'd see high AG acidosis and stop. The calculation reveals concurrent alkalosis, guiding fluid choice (NS not LR) and potassium repletion strategy.

cards.front: The A-a gradient widens with increasing FiO₂, making it unreliable on supplemental O₂. Use the [___] ratio instead.
cards.context:
Higher FiO₂ raises PAO₂ disproportionately faster than PaO₂ — a healthy lung on FiO₂ 1.0 has an A-a of ~100, not 10. So 'A-a 319' on 60% O₂ doesn't tell you the patient is 30× sicker than someone with A-a 10 on room air.

The P/F ratio (PaO₂ ÷ FiO₂) flattens out the FiO₂ effect: it's the standard for ARDS classification (Berlin) and for tracking ventilated patients across changes in support.

Rule of thumb: A-a on room air; P/F on any supplemental O₂.

cards.front: Normal arterial pCO₂ range is [___] mmHg.
cards.context:
PaCO₂ 35-45 mmHg = normocapnia. CO₂ is the primary respiratory acid; minute ventilation directly controls it.

>45 = hypercapnia (hypoventilation: CNS depression, neuromuscular weakness, COPD, sleep-disordered breathing). <35 = hypocapnia (hyperventilation: anxiety, pain, hypoxia, salicylate toxicity, sepsis, pregnancy).

cards.front: Delta ratio >2.0 indicates HAGMA plus [___] (e.g. DKA + vomiting).
cards.context: A delta ratio >2.0 is clinically important because it reveals a hidden metabolic alkalosis that would otherwise be masked by the acidosis.

cards.front: First-line treatment for convulsive status epilepticus is [___] 5-10 mg IV.
cards.context:
Benzodiazepines work by potentiating GABA-A receptor inhibition, hyperpolarising neurons and stopping seizure propagation.

Each minute of ongoing seizure activity worsens neuronal injury and reduces benzodiazepine efficacy (receptor internalisation), so dose early and adequately — under-dosing is the most common error.

cards.front: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI) threshold for paracetamol over 48 hours is ≥[___] g or ≥300 mg/kg.
cards.context:
This patient took 10 g over 48 hours. She is 65 kg, so 154 mg/kg over 48 hours — does not meet the over 300 mg/kg criterion.

However, she is nauseated and vomiting AND taking above therapeutic doses for over 48 hours, so she meets RSTI criteria and needs ALT and paracetamol level checked.

cards.front: In variceal bleeding, target Hb [___] g/L; over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding risk.
cards.context:
Variceal bleeding is the one setting where transfusing 'more, sooner' actively kills.

Unique to portal hypertensive bleeding (in ACS or trauma the balance tips back to higher targets).

cards.front: RSTI NAC thresholds: paracetamol >20 mg/L OR ALT >[___] U/L. The nomogram does NOT apply to RSTI.
cards.context: RSTI management differs from acute overdose — the nomogram doesn't apply. Instead, use screening labs and clinical criteria to guide NAC.

cards.front: Septic shock (Sepsis-3): vasopressors needed for MAP ≥[___] AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids.
cards.context:
Sepsis-3 (2016) split sepsis (suspected infection + organ dysfunction) from septic shock (sepsis + circulatory failure requiring vasopressor + cellular dysoxia).

Mortality in septic shock is >40% — substantially higher than sepsis without shock. Rapid escalation (Hour-1 bundle) is the response: cultures, antibiotics, fluids 30 mL/kg, vasopressors to MAP ≥65, ICU referral.

cards.front: Heart rate from a regular ECG: rate = 300 divided by the number of [___] between R waves.
cards.context:
ECG paper at standard speed runs 25 mm/s, so each large box (5 mm) is 0.2 seconds. Five large boxes = 1 second; 300 large boxes = 1 minute (300 × 0.2 s = 60 s).

Useful memorised landmarks: 1 box = 300/min, 2 = 150, 3 = 100, 4 = 75, 5 = 60, 6 = 50. Only valid for regular rhythms — for irregular rhythms (e.g., AF) count R waves in the 10-second strip and multiply by 6.

cards.front: Normal sinus rhythm requires a [___] wave before every QRS with a rate of 60-100 bpm.
cards.context:
Two diagnostic criteria for sinus rhythm: a P wave preceding every QRS, and the P wave is upright in lead II (because depolarisation travels from SA node toward the apex, in lead II's positive direction).

60-100 is convention not physiology — trained adults sit in the 40s without pathology, septic patients run 110 sinus.

cards.front: D-dimer sensitivity for PE decreases after 72 hours of symptoms because clot maturation reduces [___].
cards.context: D-dimer sensitivity decreases with time because as clots mature and organise, fibrinolysis slows and less D-dimer is released.

cards.front: In suspected ruptured AAA, target systolic BP is [___] mmHg to prevent dislodging the retroperitoneal clot.
cards.context:
Permissive hypotension (target SBP 80-90 mmHg) preserves the fragile retroperitoneal clot tamponading the rupture — restoring 'normal' BP can convert a contained leak into free int…

Practical proxy: keep them awake and talking. Aggressive fluid resuscitation also dilutes clotting factors and worsens trauma-induced coagulopathy.

cards.front: In late paracetamol overdose (>8 hours), start [___] immediately without waiting for levels.
cards.context:
NAC replenishes hepatic glutathione, which detoxifies the toxic NAPQI metabolite produced when normal sulphation/glucuronidation pathways are saturated by the overdose.

Don't anchor on the rumack-Matthew nomogram in delayed presentations; treat first and stop NAC only if level + ALT are reassuringly normal.

cards.front: Ventilator-induced respiratory alkalosis is corrected by decreasing respiratory rate or [___] to reduce minute ventilation.
cards.context:
Minute ventilation = tidal volume × respiratory rate, and CO₂ elimination scales with minute ventilation.

The downsides of iatrogenic alkalosis are real: cerebral vasoconstriction (worse cerebral O₂ delivery, important in TBI), left-shift of the oxyhaemoglobin curve (less O₂ released to tissues).

cards.front: Key damage control resuscitation targets: pH greater than 7.2, lactate less than 4 mmol/L, ionised calcium greater than [___] mmol/L, and temperature greater than 35°C.
cards.context:
Resuscitation targets during damage control provide specific endpoints to guide product replacement. These numbers should be checked every 30-60 minutes during active MTP.

TBI patients have higher targets because the injured brain tolerates coagulopathy and anaemia poorly.

cards.front: Large-volume [___] causes hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis due to Cl concentration of 154 mmol/L.
cards.context:
Plasma Cl ~100 mmol/L; normal saline is 154 — every litre dumps a chloride load the kidneys must dispose of. When load outpaces excretion, Cl displaces HCO₃ → non-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis.

Signature: falling pH + HCO₃, climbing Cl, normal AG after a few litres of saline. Fix: switch to balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) matching plasma Cl.

cards.front: Dobutamine starting dose is [___] mcg/kg/min.
cards.context: Beta-1 receptors in the heart increase both contractility (force) and chronotropy (rate). The downside is tachyarrhythmias — watch for AF and VT, especially above 10 mcg/kg/min.

cards.front: In FASTHUG-BID, the 'D' stands for De-escalation — review cultures at [___] hours and narrow antibiotic spectrum.
cards.context:
ICU antibiotic stewardship rests on one principle: broad-spectrum empiric therapy is appropriate only until cultures and trajectory let you narrow. Holding broad cover drives resistance, C. difficile, and candidaemia.

FASTHUG-BID reserves a daily slot at 48-72 h for de-escalation — by then sensitivities are usually back and you can swap to the narrowest effective drug.

cards.front: Monitoring frequency for IV maintenance fluids: check U&E at least every [___] hours; more often if electrolytes are abnormal.
cards.context:
Guidelines (NICE CG174 / RCH) advise checking U&E at least daily while a patient is on IV maintenance fluids — and more often (e.g. 4–6 hourly) if electrolytes are already abnormal or the patient is unstable.

Daily monitoring catches insidious hyponatraemia early.
